title: Article. The Investment Matching Principle: How the Risk/ Return Profile Connects to Diversification
summary:
This week's memo title is the investment matching principle, how the risk
return profile connects to diversification. Warren Buffett famously issues excessive diversification, but he also focuses
on investments that have very little risk of impairment of capital. A successful investor can be one who diversifies
a lot or a little, but it will always be someone who matches risk of impairment of capital
with the number of independent investments they make.

the adieu. This week's memo title is the investment matching principle, how the risk
return profile connects to diversification. First section. Intro. Inherent in every financial instrument
is a certain probability of various returns or losses. It is commonly believed that it is the
instrument itself, whether that be stocks, options, bonds, etc., that determine whether ownership of such
instrument is wise. But, that is not always the case. Should you write just a single
earthquake insurance policy that if you had a payout would bankrupt you, then you have made a terrible error of judgment.
However, if you write a thousand such policies across a wide geographic area, then that could be
financially savvy. The key difference is two concepts. One, diversification and two, conjunctive probabilities.
Warren Buffett famously issues excessive diversification, but he also focuses
on investments that have very little risk of impairment of capital. A successful investor can be one who diversifies
a lot or a little, but it will always be someone who matches risk of impairment of capital
with the number of independent investments they make. The reason for this is because
on a long enough time horizon, what can happen will happen. Should an investor have too few
independently correlated investments, they risk incurring losses too high to come back
from. We will clarify later that correlated investments are those with related risks, not price movements. But first,
bonds. Next section. Building a portfolio of bonds. Let's assume that if a bond defaults, it will be worth
0, i.e. assuming no recovery. This allows us to create a fairly binary outcome.
Either you get your principal and coupon, or it defaults and you get nothing. Now, the return profile
profile isn't really in the question here. The return a bondholder will get, assuming no default or early
sale, is going to only be the stated coupon. There is no chance that it returns more,
and outside a default, it won't return less. If we say that a portfolio of bonds
has a 5% chance of default, then the question is, what return will you demand from
this portfolio and how many individual bonds would you need in order to be adequately diversified?
At the extreme, if you own just a single bond, then there is a possibility that you lose all of your money.
If you have 100 bonds, but only demand a coupon of 3%, then it is highly likely that you not only
won't make any money, but we'll lose a little. There are three mistakes that an investor can make.
purchasing a bond portfolio without a high enough yield to compensate for the default rate,
estimating the default rate incorrectly, and not having a high enough number of bonds that are
independently correlated. With a risk-free rate of 4%, the investor would look for a yield of
at least 9%, so the income offsets the expected defaults, and they still make the risk-free rate.
The default rate of 5% though is an average, and if the bonds share exposure to common risk,
than a much larger number of bonds could default in a given year.
As the saying goes, never forget the six-foot-tall man who drowned, crossing the stream that was four feet
deep on average.
Should this investor have a portfolio of 40 bonds that are all underridden by various Gulf Coast energy
companies with break-even oil cost over $60, $60, this investor may have 40 individual
securities, but any event that causes oil prices to fall or production to stop on the Gulf Coast,
could ruin them. While this is a fairly contrived example, the point is that portfolio
diversification should be thought about in terms of commonly shared risks. The reason for this is because
proper diversification reduces conjunctive probabilities. Next section. Conjunctive probabilities. A
Conjunctive probability is the probability of two or more events occurring simultaneously.
Or, in technical terms, it's where the two circles overlap in the graph below.
If the probability of event A and event B are 5%, then the probability of both occurring is
0.25%. The general idea is that if you have a portfolio of multiple investments, the probability
that something will go wrong with multiple investments simultaneously is much less
than the probability that something will go wrong with any one investment.
A condition of this being true, though, is independence, and few investments are truly independent.
Next section. True uncorrelation is rare. Now, most investors have heard of not over-concentrating in one sector,
but the real thing they should focus on is the underlying risk each investment shares.
You may own a bunch of China stocks and think you are a diversified owning Apple,
But you would be mistaken, as the majority of their supply chain is based in China, as well as 20% of their sales.
Snapchat, Meta, Pinterest, and Twitter, all had the same data privacy and mobile platform risk.
ATT impacted all of them to a degree.
Owning nothing but U.S. pharmaceutical companies puts you at risk of health care legislation impacting all of your holdings.
Minimum wage laws may hit restaurants and retailers particularly hard.
It's not about the sector each company is in per se.
but the fact that the same event can adversely impact each company.
This is essentially the lesson of the great financial crisis.
Do not assume something is uncorrelated, just because something like the geography is different.
When investors bought mortgage-backed securities, MBS, they were taught to believe that grouping together
a bunch of individual mortgages across different income stratums, geographies, home types, etc.,
would mean that the likelihood of the whole portfolio of mortgages defaulting all at once was lowered.
This, of course, was erroneous because all of these mortgages were exposed to the same risk,
the necessity of home prices increasing in order to avoid default.
What these MBS investors conceptualized as a highly diversified bet across different income levels
and geographies was really a single bet on home prices never falling.
This is all to say that an investor must look at the common risk their portfolio of companies
are exposed to. Some commonly shared risk are unavoidable, like taxes increasing
for U.S. companies, or near unavoidable, like oil prices increasing, which could adversely
impact not just an airline or a cruise operator, but also a petrochemical manufacturer and food producer.
However, rising oil prices could be a positive for other businesses, like an E&P producer or
manufacturer. Now, the point is not to look for adverse events and see what you can own in
order to offset that risk, but rather, just to be aware of how exposed your
portfolio is to a given risk. If an offset happens to exist, then that risk is somewhat mitigated.
Berkshire pays out a lot of insurance claims when storms rip through communities, but they also own

and tack payments, but as an owner of both, you become somewhat more neutral to the outcome
in these negotiations. It would be poor practice to purchase any business.
just because it stood to benefit should a risk manifest in a separate business, but it could

lower risk of their cash flows materially disappearing or their business becoming obsolete than, say,
Peloton or Crocs.
The second method to account for risk in a portfolio is with positioning and the number of independent
investments you have.
You would need fewer, quote, CMEs in your portfolio to adequately diversify than you would need
crocs, which just narrowly avoided bankrupt.
in 2009. On the other hand, the possibility that Crox becomes a much bigger business

that will either triple or go to zero with a 50-50 probability of each event

This portfolio has an expected return of 50%.
